description: We are a team of technology enthusiasts passionate about using Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, and innovative software solutions to address real-world challenges. Our team brings together experience in software engineering, machine learning, data analytics, and application development. We aim to transform scientific ideas and NASA data into practical, impactful solutions through collaboration, creativity, and problem-solving.
summary: On the way to Mars, help from Earth is up to 20 minutes away, so astronauts must spot health problems themselves. AstroTwin is a health monitoring dashboard that learns each astronaut's personal normal from a 1-minute daily check-in. Machine learning (rolling personal baselines plus an Isolation Forest) flags unusual days, and five gauges track NASA's key risks: bone, cardiovascular, immune, behavioral and radiation. Real solar flares and particle events from NASA's DONKI database trigger shelter alerts. Every alert comes with plain-language actions. On a simulated 180-day Mars mission, AstroTwin caught 8 of 8 hidden health events with a 2% false-alarm rate.
details:
What it does AstroTwin turns a 1-minute daily check-in (resting heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, exercise, mood, symptoms) into early warnings. Instead of comparing astronauts to a population average, it compares each person with their own previous 14 days. Heart rate of 66 bpm may be normal for one crew member and a warning sign for another.

How it works?

Personal baselines: rolling z-scores per astronaut and per measurement, using only past days.

Anomaly detection: one Isolation Forest per astronaut finds days that are unusual across several measurements at once. A flag is kept only when at least one measurement is clearly outside the personal normal.

Risk scores (0–100) for five NASA human-health risk areas: bone loss, cardiovascular change, immune stress, behavioral health and radiation exposure.

Space weather: real solar flares, geomagnetic storms and solar energetic particle events from NASA DONKI are placed on the mission timeline and trigger shelter alerts.

Guidance: each alert says what to do next, for example rest and re-check, protect the next sleep period, or book a private call home.

Results: We hid 8 health events (illness, insomnia, heart-rate spikes) across 13 days in a simulated 180-day mission for a crew of 4. AstroTwin caught all 8 events and 12 of 13 bad days, with 13 false alarms in 664 monitored days (2.0%). We tuned it to miss nothing: on a Mars mission, a missed illness costs more than an extra check-in.

Mission replay: A slider moves through all 180 days. Mission day 90 is 10 May 2024, when NASA DONKI recorded X-class solar flares and a burst of energetic particles. The dashboard shows the shelter alert, the radiation gauge jumping, the month-4 behavioral slump and bone loss building over six months.

Benefits: Astronauts get early, personal warnings without waiting for Earth. The same approach helps people on Earth who live far from a doctor: polar and submarine crews, remote workers, and older adults living alone.

Tools: Python, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, Plotly, Next.js, requests. Deployed on Vercel. Code is open source on GitHub.

Limitations: Astronaut health data is simulated because real records are private. Risk weights are hand-set.

Next steps: test on public wearable datasets and calibrate risk scores with clinical input.
